prompt: The Stamp Act of 1765 made American colonists buy a government stamp for what?
choices: Legal documents and other paper goods
explain: The Stamp Act taxed paper items like legal documents. Colonists protested so strongly that Britain repealed it.

prompt: During the Boston Tea Party in December 1773, colonists threw what into Boston Harbor?
explain: Colonists dumped crates of tea into the harbor to protest British control of the tea trade. Britain answered by closing the port of Boston.

prompt: The first battles of the American Revolution, at Lexington and Concord, were fought in which year?
explain: The fighting at Lexington and Concord happened on April 19, 1775. It was the first battle of the American Revolution.

prompt: Who wrote the original draft of the Declaration of Independence?
explain: Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft. Benjamin Franklin and John Adams helped edit it before it went to Congress.

prompt: On what date did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
explain: Congress adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776. That is why the Fourth of July is Independence Day.

prompt: Who wrote Common Sense, the 1776 pamphlet that urged the colonies to break away from Britain?
explain: Thomas Paine wrote Common Sense, first printed in January 1776. It argued that separating from Britain was the only sensible choice.

prompt: The Battle of Bunker Hill (June 17, 1775) is named for Bunker Hill, but most of the fighting took place on which nearby hill?
explain: Most of the fighting was on Breed's Hill, right next to Bunker Hill. The British took the hill but lost many soldiers.

prompt: Which British general surrendered his whole army at Saratoga in 1777?
explain: General John Burgoyne surrendered his army at Saratoga. It was the first time a whole British army had ever surrendered.

prompt: News of the American victory at Saratoga convinced which country to sign an alliance with the United States in 1778?
explain: After Saratoga, France decided to ally with the Americans. The Treaty of Alliance was signed in February 1778.

prompt: George Washington's Continental Army spent the hard winter of 1777-78 camped at Valley Forge in which present-day state?
explain: Valley Forge is in Pennsylvania. The Continental Army camped there through the winter of 1777-78.

prompt: In 1781, which British general surrendered to American and French forces at Yorktown, Virginia?
explain: General Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown on October 19, 1781. It was the last major battle of the Revolutionary War.

prompt: What did Britain accept in the Treaty of Paris, signed in 1783?
choices: The sale of Louisiana to the United States
The end of the War of 1812
The return of Texas to Mexico
explain: In the Treaty of Paris, Britain accepted American independence and new boundaries. It formally ended the Revolutionary War.

prompt: What was a major weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation?
choices: It had a very large army
explain: Under the Articles, the central government could not tax and had little power over trade. These weaknesses led to the Constitutional Convention.

prompt: In which city did delegates meet in 1787 to write the U.S. Constitution?
explain: The Constitutional Convention met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia. Today that building is called Independence Hall.

prompt: What did the Great Compromise of 1787 decide about how states are represented in Congress?
choices: Every state gets the same number of seats in both houses
Only large states get seats in the Senate
House seats are based on population, and each state gets equal seats in the Senate
explain: The Great Compromise gave the House seats based on population. It gave every state the same number of seats in the Senate.

prompt: How many states had to ratify (approve) the Constitution before it went into effect?
explain: The Constitution needed 9 of the 13 states to approve it. New Hampshire became the ninth state in 1788.

prompt: Who wrote most of the Federalist Papers, the essays that urged people to support the new Constitution?
explain: Alexander Hamilton wrote most of the 85 Federalist essays. James Madison and John Jay also took part.

prompt: Which founder is often called the "Father of the Constitution"?
explain: James Madison drafted the Virginia Plan and took detailed notes at the Convention. That is why he is called the Father of the Constitution.

prompt: In what year were the first ten amendments to the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, ratified?
explain: Ten of the twelve proposed amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791. Together they are called the Bill of Rights.

prompt: Which rights does the First Amendment protect?
choices: Freedom of religion, speech, and the press
The right to vote at age 18
Equal seats for every state in the Senate
explain: The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, assembly, and petition. It is part of the Bill of Rights.

prompt: Which branch of the U.S. government makes the laws?
explain: The legislative branch, Congress, makes the laws. Congress is made up of the House and the Senate.

prompt: Where did George Washington take the oath of office as the first president in April 1789?
explain: Washington took the oath at Federal Hall in New York City on April 30, 1789. Washington, D.C., did not exist as the capital yet.

prompt: Who was the first Secretary of the Treasury of the United States?
explain: Alexander Hamilton became the first Secretary of the Treasury in 1789. He served until 1795.

prompt: The Supreme Court case Marbury v. Madison (1803) set up which important power?
choices: The power of the president to veto bills
The power of Congress to declare war
The power of states to print money
Judicial review: the power of courts to strike down laws that go against the Constitution
explain: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion established judicial review. It means courts can decide if a law breaks the Constitution.

prompt: From which country did the United States buy the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
explain: The United States bought Louisiana from France for $15 million. The purchase roughly doubled the size of the country.

prompt: Which president made the Louisiana Purchase in 1803?
explain: Thomas Jefferson was president during the Louisiana Purchase. He went ahead even though he was unsure the Constitution allowed it.

prompt: Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery left St. Louis in 1804. Which ocean did they reach in November 1805?
explain: The expedition reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805. They returned to St. Louis in September 1806.

prompt: Sacagawea, who helped the Lewis and Clark expedition, belonged to which Native American people?
explain: Sacagawea was Lemhi Shoshone. She helped the expedition talk with the Shoshone and recognized landmarks near her childhood home.

prompt: In the War of 1812, the United States fought against which country?
explain: The United States declared war on Great Britain in 1812. One cause was Britain forcing American sailors into its navy.

prompt: Francis Scott Key wrote the poem that became "The Star-Spangled Banner" after watching the British bombard which fort in 1814?
explain: Key saw the American flag still flying over Fort McHenry in Baltimore. His poem later became the national anthem.

prompt: Which treaty, signed on December 24, 1814, ended the War of 1812?
explain: The Treaty of Ghent ended the War of 1812. It put the borders back the way they were before the war.

prompt: What did the Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warn European countries not to do?
choices: Set up new colonies in the Americas
Sell land to the United States
explain: President James Monroe warned Europe against starting new colonies in the Western Hemisphere. Secretary of State John Quincy Adams helped shape the idea.

prompt: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, connected which two bodies of water?
choices: The Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico
The Ohio River and Lake Michigan
The Hudson River and Lake Erie
explain: The Erie Canal opened on October 26, 1825, and linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie. It made shipping goods between the East and the Great Lakes much easier.

prompt: Which president signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830?
explain: Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act on May 28, 1830. It led to tribes being moved west of the Mississippi River.

prompt: On the Trail of Tears in 1838-39, the Cherokee were forced to move to Indian Territory. Where is that land today?
explain: The Cherokee were forced from their homelands in the Southeast to Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma. Thousands died on the journey.

prompt: The first women's rights convention was held in 1848 in Seneca Falls, in which state?
explain: The convention met in Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19-20, 1848. About 300 people came, including Frederick Douglass.

prompt: Elizabeth Cady Stanton helped write which document at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention?
explain: Stanton and the M'Clintock family drafted the Declaration of Sentiments. It was signed by 68 women and 32 men.

prompt: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in 1848, ended which war?
explain: The treaty ended the Mexican-American War. Mexico gave up land that includes present-day California, Nevada, and Utah.

prompt: People who rushed to California in 1849 to look for gold were given what nickname?
explain: Gold was found in California in January 1848. The crowds who came looking for it in 1849 were called Forty-Niners.

prompt: Under the Missouri Compromise of 1820, how did Missouri and Maine enter the Union?
choices: Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state
Missouri as a free state and Maine as a slave state
explain: Missouri came in as a slave state and Maine as a free state. That kept the number of slave and free states equal.

prompt: Under the Compromise of 1850, California entered the Union as what?
explain: Congress admitted California as a free state in 1850. The same compromise also passed a stricter Fugitive Slave Act.

prompt: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers in those territories vote to decide what?
explain: Senator Stephen Douglas's act let settlers decide on slavery, an idea called popular sovereignty. Fighting over this in Kansas earned the name "Bleeding Kansas."

prompt: Who wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin, the 1852 novel that showed the cruelty of slavery?
explain: Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin. It became a best seller and drew attention to slavery, especially families being torn apart.

prompt: In the Dred Scott decision of 1857, what did the Supreme Court rule?
choices: Slavery was illegal everywhere in the country
Enslaved people and their descendants were not U.S. citizens and could not sue in federal court
Kansas had to be a free state
Women had the right to vote
explain: Chief Justice Roger Taney's ruling said Black Americans were not citizens. The 14th Amendment later overturned this idea.

prompt: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in which state before escaping to freedom in 1849?
explain: Tubman was born on Maryland's Eastern Shore and escaped to Philadelphia in 1849. She went back 13 times and led more than 70 people to freedom.

prompt: Frederick Douglass founded which anti-slavery newspaper in 1847?
explain: Douglass founded and edited The North Star. Its name came from the star that guided people escaping slavery to the North.

prompt: What is the title of the 1845 book Frederick Douglass wrote about his life?
choices: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
explain: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass came out in 1845. It was the first of three books he wrote about his life.

prompt: In what year was Abraham Lincoln first elected president?
explain: Lincoln won the election of 1860 and became the 16th president. Seven Southern states left the Union before he took office.

prompt: Who was the president of the Confederate States of America?
explain: Jefferson Davis was the Confederacy's president. Before the war he was a U.S. senator from Mississippi.

prompt: The Civil War began in April 1861 when Confederates fired on Fort Sumter. Where was Fort Sumter?
explain: Fort Sumter sits in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina. The first shots of the Civil War were fired there on April 12, 1861.

prompt: On what date did President Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
explain: Lincoln issued it on January 1, 1863. It declared enslaved people in the rebelling states free and let Black men join the Union Army and Navy.

prompt: The Battle of Gettysburg, fought July 1-3, 1863, took place in which state?
explain: Gettysburg is in Pennsylvania. It was the bloodiest battle of the Civil War and ended Lee's hopes of invading the North.

prompt: President Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address in November 1863 at what event?
choices: The dedication of a cemetery for soldiers killed at Gettysburg
The opening of the transcontinental railroad
explain: Lincoln spoke on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers killed in the battle.

prompt: Where did Robert E. Lee surrender his Army of Northern Virginia on April 9, 1865?
explain: The surrender took place in the McLean House at Appomattox Court House, Virginia. Lee met there with General Ulysses S. Grant.

prompt: Who assassinated President Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in April 1865?
explain: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865. Lincoln died at the Petersen House across the street.

prompt: Which amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery in the United States?
explain: The 13th Amendment abolished slavery. It was ratified on December 6, 1865.

prompt: The 14th Amendment (1868) made citizens of whom?
choices: Only people born in the original 13 states
All persons born or naturalized in the United States
explain: The 14th Amendment made all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. citizens, including formerly enslaved people. It also promises equal protection of the laws.

prompt: What did the 15th Amendment (1870) say about voting?
choices: Women must be allowed to vote
The right to vote cannot be denied because of race, color, or having been enslaved
explain: The 15th Amendment stopped governments from denying the vote because of race, color, or past slavery. It gave African American men the right to vote.

prompt: What was the main job of the Freedmen's Bureau, created in 1865?
choices: To collect taxes from the South
To help formerly enslaved people with food, schools, medical care, and legal help
To train soldiers for the Union Army
explain: The Freedmen's Bureau helped formerly enslaved people start new lives. It gave food, housing, medical aid, schools, and legal help.

prompt: Which president did the House of Representatives impeach in 1868?
explain: The House voted 126 to 47 to impeach Andrew Johnson in February 1868. The Senate fell one vote short of removing him from office.

prompt: After gold was found near present-day Denver in the late 1850s, Congress created what new territory on February 28, 1861?
explain: The gold rush brought many settlers to the area. Congress formed Colorado Territory on February 28, 1861.

prompt: Colorado became the 38th state on August 1, 1876. Why is it called the Centennial State?
choices: It was the 100th place settled in the West
It became a state 100 years after the Declaration of Independence
explain: Centennial means 100 years. Colorado became a state in 1876, 100 years after the Declaration of Independence in 1776.

prompt: On November 29, 1864, soldiers led by Colonel John Chivington attacked a camp at Sand Creek in Colorado Territory. Which peoples lived in that camp?
explain: The camp at Sand Creek was home to Cheyenne and Arapaho people. More than 230 were killed, many of them women, children, and elders.

prompt: The Mason-Dixon line was surveyed in the 1760s to mark the border between which two colonies?
explain: Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon were hired in 1763 to settle the border between Maryland and Pennsylvania. They ran their survey lines from 1764 to 1767. Later it was seen as the line between free states and slave states.

prompt: Primary sources are created at the time being studied. Which of these is a primary source about the Civil War?
choices: A photograph taken at a battlefield in 1863
An encyclopedia article written last year
explain: A photo taken in 1863 was made during the war, so it is a primary source. The others were made long after and explain the past, so they are secondary sources.

prompt: In 1774 Parliament passed laws to punish Massachusetts and put it under direct British control. What did American colonists call these laws?
explain: The 1774 laws tried to put Massachusetts under direct British control. Colonists called them the Intolerable Acts.

prompt: When the First Continental Congress met in the fall of 1774, what did it call for?
explain: The Congress met in September 1774. It listed the colonies' complaints and called for a boycott of British goods.

prompt: The Declaration of Independence says all people have certain unalienable rights. Which three does it name?
choices: Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness
explain: The Declaration names Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness. Unalienable means they cannot be taken away.

prompt: According to the Declaration of Independence, where do governments get their just powers?
choices: From the divine right of kings
From the strength of the army
From the consent of the governed
explain: The Declaration says governments get their just powers from the consent of the governed. That means the people agree to be governed.

prompt: On June 7, 1776, which Virginia delegate proposed in Congress that the colonies should be free and independent states?
explain: Richard Henry Lee presented the Lee Resolution on June 7, 1776. Congress approved it on July 2.

prompt: Congress voted for independence two days before it adopted the Declaration of Independence. On what date was that vote?
explain: Congress approved the Lee Resolution for independence on July 2, 1776. It adopted the Declaration on July 4.

prompt: Who was President of the Continental Congress and signed the Declaration of Independence first, with a large bold signature?
explain: John Hancock was President of the Congress. He signed first, in the center below the text.

prompt: In 1786, Daniel Shays led armed farmers in an uprising in which state?
explain: Shays and the farmers blocked a court in Northampton, Massachusetts, and threatened the Springfield arsenal. State troops put the uprising down.

prompt: The Three-Fifths Compromise at the 1787 Constitutional Convention was about what?
choices: How to count enslaved people when deciding a state's representation
How many states had to approve the Constitution
How many senators each state would get
How long a president could serve
explain: Delegates agreed to count three-fifths of enslaved people when deciding representation. The Constitution used the words 'all other persons' to mean enslaved people.

prompt: On what date did the delegates sign the U.S. Constitution?
explain: The Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787, in Philadelphia.

prompt: Who did the delegates elect to lead (preside over) the Constitutional Convention in 1787?
explain: The delegates elected George Washington president of the Convention on May 25, 1787. The vote was unanimous.

prompt: What was a main complaint the Anti-Federalists had about the new Constitution?
choices: It let the King of Britain veto laws
It did not allow states to have governors
It made the president serve for life
It had no bill of rights to protect individual freedoms
explain: Anti-Federalists said the Constitution needed a bill of rights. The first ten amendments were added in 1791.

prompt: Who presented the New Jersey Plan, which would have mostly revised the Articles of Confederation instead of creating a new national government?
explain: William Paterson offered the New Jersey Plan in June 1787. The Convention debated it and rejected it.

prompt: How long is a term for a member of the U.S. House of Representatives?
explain: The Constitution says House members are chosen every second year. That makes a term 2 years.

prompt: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
explain: The Constitution gives senators a term of six years. Senators serve longer terms than House members.

prompt: Under the Constitution, how many senators does each state get?
choices: It depends on the state's population
explain: Each state gets two senators no matter its size. House seats, not Senate seats, depend on population.

prompt: What is the minimum age to be president of the United States, according to the Constitution?
explain: The Constitution says a president must be at least 35 years old. Senators must be 30 and House members 25.

prompt: How long is one presidential term under the Constitution?
explain: Article II sets the president's term at four years.

prompt: If the president vetoes a bill, Congress can still make it a law. What vote does that take?
choices: A simple majority of each house
Two-thirds of each house of Congress
A unanimous vote of the Senate
explain: Congress can override a veto if two-thirds of each house votes for the bill. This is one of the checks and balances.

prompt: Before a treaty made by the president can take effect, who must approve it?
choices: A majority of the House of Representatives
explain: The president makes treaties with the advice and consent of the Senate. Two-thirds of the senators present must agree.

prompt: Which part of Congress has the power to impeach (formally charge) a federal official?
explain: The Constitution gives the House the sole power of impeachment. The Senate then holds the trial.

prompt: Who presides over the Senate trial when a president is impeached?
choices: The Chief Justice of the United States
explain: The Constitution says the Chief Justice presides when the president is tried.

prompt: After Congress proposes an amendment, how many of the states must ratify it before it becomes part of the Constitution?
explain: Article V says three-fourths of the states must ratify an amendment. Two-thirds of both houses of Congress propose it.

prompt: Under the Constitution, who is Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy?
explain: Article II makes the president Commander in Chief.

prompt: Under the Constitution, which branch has the power to declare war?
explain: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war. The president commands the military, but Congress declares war.

prompt: Which amendment protects the right of the people to keep and bear arms?
explain: The Second Amendment protects the right to keep and bear arms. It is part of the Bill of Rights.

prompt: Which amendment says soldiers cannot be housed in a private home in peacetime without the owner's permission?
explain: The Third Amendment bans quartering soldiers in homes in peacetime without consent.

prompt: Which amendment protects people from unreasonable searches and seizures?
explain: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. A warrant needs probable cause.

prompt: Which amendment protects a person from being tried twice for the same crime (called double jeopardy)?
explain: The Fifth Amendment bars double jeopardy. It also protects people from having to testify against themselves.

prompt: The Sixth Amendment gives a person accused of a crime the right to what?
explain: The Sixth Amendment promises a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury. It also guarantees a lawyer for the defense.

prompt: Which amendment bans "cruel and unusual punishments"?
explain: The Eighth Amendment bans cruel and unusual punishments. It also bans excessive bail and fines.

prompt: The Tenth Amendment says powers not given to the national government are reserved to whom?
explain: The Tenth Amendment reserves those powers to the states or to the people. It limits the national government.

prompt: Baron von Steuben trained the Continental Army at Valley Forge. He had been an officer in the army of which European country?
explain: Von Steuben was born in Prussia and served in the Prussian Army. At Valley Forge he created standard drills for the whole army.

prompt: What did the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 say about slavery in the Northwest Territory?
choices: Slavery was allowed and protected there
explain: The Ordinance said there shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the territory. It also set up how new states would form there.

prompt: Under the Articles of Confederation, how many votes did each state have in Congress?
choices: One for each delegate it sent
explain: Article V of the Articles gave each state one vote, no matter its population. A state could send two to seven delegates.

prompt: Under the Articles of Confederation, what was needed to change (amend) the Articles?
choices: A ruling by the national courts
explain: Changes needed Congress and the legislature of every state to agree.

prompt: Which president signed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798?
explain: President John Adams signed the acts, which a Federalist Congress passed. Democratic-Republican editors were the ones prosecuted.

prompt: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court ruled that Maryland could not do what?
choices: Collect taxes from its own citizens
Tax the Second Bank of the United States
explain: The Court said Congress could create the bank and Maryland could not tax it. Chief Justice Marshall wrote that "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."

prompt: The Supreme Court case Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) was about a New York monopoly on what?
explain: New York gave Robert Fulton and Robert Livingston a steamboat monopoly. The Court ruled that Congress regulates trade between the states.

prompt: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered a settler how many acres of public land?
explain: The act granted a quarter section, which is 160 acres. Settlers had to live on and farm the land.

prompt: Which two companies built the first transcontinental railroad under the Pacific Railway Act?
choices: Santa Fe and Denver and Rio Grande
explain: The Pacific Railway Act of 1862 backed the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific. They built toward each other from east and west.

prompt: Where were the tracks of the first transcontinental railroad joined on May 10, 1869?
explain: The last spike was driven at Promontory, Utah, on May 10, 1869. The railroad linked the East and the West.

prompt: The Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people free in which places?
choices: In every state, North and South
Only in the border states loyal to the Union
Only in areas that were in rebellion against the Union
explain: The proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion. It did not apply to the loyal border states, where slavery remained.

prompt: The Morrill Act of 1862 used federal land to help start what?
explain: The Morrill Act funded public land-grant colleges. They taught agriculture and the mechanic arts.

prompt: Which Civil War battle, fought near Sharpsburg, Maryland, in 1862, was the single bloodiest day in U.S. history?
explain: Antietam was the single bloodiest day in U.S. history. It was part of General Lee's Maryland Campaign.

prompt: Jay's Treaty (1794) settled problems between the United States and which country?
explain: Chief Justice John Jay negotiated the treaty with Great Britain. Britain agreed to give up its forts in the Northwest.

prompt: In the XYZ Affair (1798), officials from which country demanded a bribe from American diplomats?
explain: Agents of France's foreign minister, Talleyrand, demanded a bribe. The affair led to an undeclared naval war with France called the Quasi-War.

prompt: Texas won its war for independence in 1836 against which country?
explain: Texas won independence from Mexico in 1836. It was an independent republic for almost ten years.

prompt: In what year was Texas admitted to the United States?
explain: Congress passed a joint resolution to annex Texas in March 1845. Texas was admitted on December 29, 1845.

prompt: The 1846 Oregon Treaty with Great Britain set the border at which line of latitude?
explain: The treaty set the border at the 49th parallel. Some Americans had demanded the line at 54 degrees 40 minutes.

prompt: The United States made the Gadsden Purchase from Mexico in 1853-54 mainly to get land for what?
choices: A southern route for a transcontinental railroad
explain: The land was wanted for a southern transcontinental railroad. It is now part of Arizona and New Mexico.

prompt: When British troops approached Washington, D.C., in August 1814, Dolley Madison ordered that what be saved from the White House?
choices: A full-length portrait of George Washington
explain: Dolley Madison ordered Gilbert Stuart's portrait of Washington saved on August 24, 1814. Paul Jennings, an enslaved worker, was among those who helped.

prompt: Which American general won the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815?
explain: Andrew Jackson's army won a big victory at New Orleans. It was a major battle near the end of the War of 1812.

prompt: Tecumseh, a Shawnee leader who worked to unite Native nations, fought on which side in the War of 1812?
explain: Tecumseh allied with the British. He was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813.

prompt: In his Farewell Address (1796), what did George Washington warn Americans against?
choices: Settling west of the Mississippi River
explain: Washington urged the country to steer clear of permanent foreign alliances. He also warned against political parties.

prompt: How did George Washington's Farewell Address first reach the public in 1796?
choices: It was read aloud to Congress
It was given as a speech at his second inauguration
It was sent as a letter to the King of Britain
It was printed in a newspaper
explain: It first appeared in the American Daily Advertiser newspaper on September 19, 1796. In it Washington said he would not seek a third term.

prompt: The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 was a protest by farmers in western Pennsylvania against what?
choices: A federal tax on whiskey and other distilled spirits
A ban on settling west of the mountains
explain: Congress taxed distilled spirits in 1791. Washington sent about 13,000 militiamen, and the rebellion ended without a major battle.

prompt: Before it became a fort, the Alamo in San Antonio, Texas, was what?
explain: The Alamo began as Mission San Antonio de Valero, a Spanish mission. The Battle of the Alamo ended on March 6, 1836.

prompt: Who led the Mexican army that besieged the Alamo in 1836?
explain: Mexican President Santa Anna led the siege. About 189 defenders were killed.

prompt: In 1832, South Carolina tried to nullify (cancel inside the state) which federal laws?
explain: South Carolina declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void. President Jackson answered with a proclamation and the Force Act.

prompt: Sequoyah created a writing system (a syllabary) for which language?
explain: Sequoyah created the Cherokee syllabary. Each symbol stands for a syllable, not a single letter.

prompt: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), what did the Supreme Court decide?
choices: The Cherokee Nation was a separate nation, so Georgia's laws did not apply there
The Cherokee had to move west of the Mississippi River
The Cherokee could not publish a newspaper
explain: The Court said the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community not under Georgia's laws. President Jackson did not act to enforce the ruling.

prompt: Which Cherokee chief argued against the 1835 Treaty of New Echota, which traded away Cherokee lands in the East?
explain: Cherokee Chief John Ross opposed the treaty. A small group without authority signed it, and it was ratified in 1836 anyway.

prompt: The Union capture of Vicksburg on July 4, 1863, helped the Union control which river?
explain: General Grant took Vicksburg after a 47-day siege. His goal was to secure the Mississippi River for the Union.

prompt: The 54th Massachusetts, which attacked Fort Wagner in South Carolina in 1863, was famous for being what kind of regiment?
explain: The 54th Massachusetts was an all-Black volunteer regiment led by Colonel Robert Gould Shaw. William Carney won the Medal of Honor for saving its flag.

prompt: In late 1864, General William T. Sherman marched his army across Georgia from Atlanta to which coastal city?
explain: Sherman left Atlanta on November 15, 1864. Savannah surrendered on December 22, 1864.

prompt: Confederate general Thomas Jackson got the nickname "Stonewall" at which battle?
choices: The First Battle of Bull Run
explain: At Bull Run, General Bee said Jackson was standing like a stone wall. Jackson was later shot by his own men at Chancellorsville.

prompt: Who did President Lincoln appoint in 1861 as the first governor of Colorado Territory?
explain: Lincoln appointed William Gilpin on March 22, 1861. John Evans replaced him in 1862.

prompt: In March 1862 at Glorieta Pass in New Mexico Territory, Colorado volunteers helped stop a Confederate invasion by destroying what?
explain: Union troops burned the Confederate supply wagons at Johnson's Ranch. Without supplies, the Confederates had to retreat.

prompt: Which territorial governor of Colorado was removed from office in 1865 for his role in the Sand Creek affair?
explain: A congressional committee called for Evans's removal. He was removed on August 1, 1865.

prompt: What did the 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise do to Cheyenne and Arapaho lands?
choices: It made them a separate state
It gave them all of Colorado Territory
explain: The treaty drastically shrank Cheyenne and Arapaho lands. Most of their chiefs refused to sign it.

prompt: Bent's Fort, an adobe trading post built in 1833 in what is now southeastern Colorado, stood on which river?
explain: William and Charles Bent and Ceran St. Vrain built the fort on the Arkansas River. It was a major stop on the Santa Fe Trail.

prompt: William Lloyd Garrison published which abolitionist newspaper in Boston starting in 1831?
explain: Garrison's Liberator demanded an immediate end to slavery. It stopped in 1865 after the 13th Amendment ended slavery.

prompt: In 1851, Sojourner Truth gave her most famous speech at a convention in Akron, Ohio. What was the convention about?
explain: Truth spoke at the Woman's Rights Convention in Akron on May 29, 1851. She was born enslaved in New York.

prompt: In October 1859, John Brown and his followers seized the federal armory in which town, hoping to start a war against slavery?
explain: Brown raided Harpers Ferry on October 16, 1859. U.S. Marines captured him, and he was hanged that December.

prompt: The seven Lincoln-Douglas debates of 1858 were part of a race for which office?
explain: Lincoln challenged Stephen Douglas for one of Illinois' Senate seats. Lincoln lost that election to Douglas.

prompt: Which state was the first to secede (leave the Union), on December 20, 1860?
explain: South Carolina seceded after Lincoln won the 1860 election. Other Southern states soon followed.

prompt: In 1870, Hiram Revels became the first African American U.S. senator. Which state did he represent?
explain: Revels was sworn in on February 25, 1870, for Mississippi. He filled a seat left empty when Southern senators withdrew in 1861.

prompt: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 divided the former Confederacy into what?
explain: Congress divided the former Confederate states into five military districts. A military governor ran each one.

prompt: What did the Wilmot Proviso of 1846 try to do?
choices: Annex Texas to the United States
End the Mexican-American War right away
Ban slavery in any land the U.S. gained from Mexico
explain: Congressman David Wilmot proposed banning slavery in land taken from Mexico. It passed the House but failed in the Senate.

prompt: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed (canceled) which earlier law about slavery?
explain: The act repealed the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which had banned slavery north of its line. Senator Stephen Douglas sponsored the act.

prompt: Which political party formed out of the anger over the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854?
explain: The turmoil over the act led to the creation of the Republican Party.

prompt: Lincoln began the Gettysburg Address in 1863 with "Four score and seven years ago." A score is 20, so he was pointing back to which year?
explain: Four score and seven is 87 years. 1863 minus 87 is 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

prompt: Who was the Republican Party's first candidate for president, in 1856?
explain: The Republicans nominated explorer John C. Fremont. Democrat James Buchanan won the election.

prompt: Which Kentucky senator first proposed the resolutions in January 1850 that led to the Compromise of 1850?
explain: Henry Clay proposed the resolutions. Stephen Douglas later passed the compromise as separate bills.

prompt: Which president asked Congress to declare war on Mexico in 1846?
explain: President Polk said Mexican troops had attacked Americans north of the Rio Grande. Congress declared war in May 1846.

prompt: The Missouri Compromise banned slavery in the Louisiana Territory north of which line?
explain: The law banned slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes, outside the new state of Missouri.

prompt: Before the Louisiana Purchase, American negotiators were first sent to France to buy which port city?
explain: The negotiators were told to buy New Orleans and the Floridas. France offered all of Louisiana instead.

prompt: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) made which river part of the border between the United States and Mexico?
explain: The treaty set the Rio Grande as the border from the Gulf of Mexico. The United States also agreed to pay Mexico $15 million.

prompt: In the Dred Scott decision (1857), what did the Supreme Court say about Congress and slavery in the territories?
choices: Congress had to ban slavery in every territory
Congress could not ban slavery in a territory
Each territory had to hold a vote on slavery
Only the president could decide about slavery
explain: Chief Justice Taney said Congress could not ban slavery in a federal territory. So Scott's move into a free territory did not make him free.
